title: How Tall Was Goliath According to the Bible?
paragraphs:
How Tall Was Goliath According to the Bible?
The Giant Was Real... But the Bigger Miracle Was Never His Height—It Was the God Who Made Him Fall.
Everyone remembers the giant.
Almost no one remembers the God who defeated him.

Ask almost any Christian—or even someone who has never opened a Bible—and they'll know the story of David and Goliath. It's become a symbol of impossible odds, underdogs, and miraculous victories. We use the phrase "David versus Goliath" for sports, business, politics, and personal struggles.
But somewhere along the way, we became fascinated with Goliath's size and forgot why Scripture tells us about him in the first place.
So...
How tall was Goliath according to the Bible?
The answer is surprisingly more fascinating—and more faith-building—than most people realize.
The traditional Hebrew text known as the Masoretic Text records in 1 Samuel 17:4:
"His height was six cubits and a span."
In Hebrew, the verse reads:

שֵׁשׁ אַמּוֹת וָזָרֶת
Shesh ammot va-zaret.
Literally:
"Six cubits and a span."

A cubit (אַמָּה, 'ammah) was the distance from the elbow to the tip of the middle finger. While its exact measurement varied slightly throughout the ancient Near East, the commonly accepted biblical cubit is about 18 inches (45.7 cm).
A span (זֶרֶת, zeret) was roughly half a cubit, approximately 9 inches (22.9 cm).
That places Goliath at approximately 9 feet 9 inches (2.97 meters) tall.
Imagine standing beside someone nearly ten feet high.
His armor alone weighed around 5,000 shekels of bronze—about 125 pounds (57 kilograms). His spearhead weighed approximately 600 shekels of iron, or about 15 pounds (6.8 kilograms) (1 Samuel 17:5–7).
Everything about him screamed one message:
"You cannot win."
And that is exactly the point.
Yet there's another fascinating detail that many believers have never heard.

One of the oldest surviving Hebrew manuscripts, preserved among the Dead Sea Scrolls (4QSamᵃ), along with the ancient Greek translation known as the Septuagint (LXX), records Goliath's height differently.
Instead of:
"Six cubits and a span,"
they read:
"Four cubits and a span."
In Greek:

τεσσάρων πήχεων καὶ σπιθαμῆς
(tessarōn pēcheōn kai spithamēs)
Literally:
"Four cubits and a span."
That would place Goliath around 6 feet 9 inches (about 2.06 meters).
For many readers, this creates an immediate question.
Which measurement is correct?
This is where careful biblical scholarship becomes important.

The Masoretic Text has been faithfully preserved for centuries and remains the basis for most English translations, including the King James Version, New King James Version, English Standard Version, and New American Standard Bible.

Meanwhile, the Dead Sea Scrolls are over a thousand years older than the oldest complete Masoretic manuscripts we possess today. Because of their age, many textual scholars believe they preserve an earlier reading of certain passages.
Neither reading changes a single doctrine of Christianity.
Neither changes the Gospel.
Neither changes God's character.
Neither changes the outcome of the story.

Whether Goliath stood nearly seven feet or nearly ten feet tall, he towered over every Israelite soldier. In an ancient world where the average man stood around five and a half feet, either height would have made him terrifying beyond imagination.
The Bible is not inviting us into a debate over inches.
It is inviting us into a revelation of faith.
Notice something remarkable.
The narrative spends far more time describing Israel's fear than Goliath's measurements.
Fear had already defeated the army before a single stone was thrown.
The giant wasn't just standing in the valley.
He was already living inside their hearts.
Then comes David.
He wasn't wearing Saul's armor.
He wasn't carrying a sword.
He had no military rank.
No impressive résumé.
No visible advantage.
He simply knew God.
When David confronted Goliath, he declared:
"You come to me with a sword and with a spear and with a javelin, but I come to you in the name of the LORD of hosts, the God of the armies of Israel, whom you have defied." (1 Samuel 17:45)
The Hebrew phrase is breathtaking:

בְּשֵׁם יְהוָה צְבָאוֹת
B'Shem YHWH Tseva'ot.
"In the Name of Yahweh of Armies."
David understood something Israel had forgotten.
Victory was never measured by the size of the warrior.
Victory belonged to the Lord.
Long before David released the stone, heaven had already decided the outcome.
This truth echoes throughout Scripture.
The Apostle Paul later reminds believers:
"For when I am weak, then I am strong." (2 Corinthians 12:10)
In Greek:

ὅταν γὰρ ἀσθενῶ, τότε δυνατός εἰμι
(Hotan gar asthenō, tote dynatos eimi.)
"When I am weak, then I am strong."
Not because weakness has power.
But because Christ does.
The greatest giant humanity has ever faced was never a Philistine champion.
It was sin.
Death.
Judgment.
No amount of human strength could defeat them.
Then Jesus Christ entered history.
He did not arrive wearing earthly armor.
He was born in a manger.
Rejected.
Mocked.
Scourged.
Crucified.
From the world's perspective, it looked like defeat.
But what looked like the greatest scandal became the greatest act of grace the universe has ever witnessed.
The empty tomb forever declared that God's victories rarely look like human victories.
This is why our theme is more than a slogan.
Perhaps the giant in your life isn't nine feet tall.
Maybe it's anxiety.
Shame.
Addiction.
Broken relationships.
Hidden sin.
A diagnosis.
Financial hardship.
Grief.
Or years of believing that God could never use someone like you.
The enemy still whispers the same lie Goliath shouted across that valley:
"You cannot win."
The Gospel answers with something far greater:
"Christ already has."
Your future is not determined by the size of your obstacle but by the greatness of your Savior.
That is the story David was pointing toward.
That is the story the cross fulfilled.
And that is the story still changing lives today.

Someone in your circle may be facing a giant they believe can never fall. The Lord may use this simple act of sharing to remind them that no battle is too great for Him. Your testimony may become the encouragement another believer has been praying for.
The giant wasn't the biggest thing in the valley—God was.
